title: Activities of Daily Living: How Communities Assess Care Needs, and Why Your Parent's Level Sets the Price
description: How Memphis-area assisted living communities assess activities of daily living, turn the result into a care level, and why that level changes the monthly price.
meta_title: Activities of Daily Living and Assisted Living Care Levels
meta_description: How assisted living communities assess bathing, dressing, medications and more, turn it into a care level, and why that level changes the monthly price.
main_html:
Quick answer

Before move-in, a nurse or wellness director from the community assesses how much help your parent needs with activities of daily living: bathing, dressing, grooming, toileting, continence, moving and transferring, and eating, plus medication management, memory and behaviour. The scores add up to a care level. Each level adds a set amount to the monthly bill, so the assessment decides a large part of what your family will pay.

Activities of daily living are the basic personal tasks of looking after yourself: bathing, dressing, eating, using the toilet, staying continent, and moving from bed to chair. Assisted living communities assess how much help a resident needs with each, add medication and memory needs, and set a care level that determines care charges.

Two parents in the same apartment at the same community can pay very different amounts because of their care levels. Knowing how the assessment works lets you check the result and plan for changes.

The activities that get scored

ActivityWhat the assessor asksExamples of more help
BathingCan your parent shower safely without help?Stand-by help, hands-on help, help every day rather than twice a week
Dressing and groomingCan they choose clothes, dress, shave, do hair?Prompting, setting out clothes, hands-on dressing
ToiletingCan they use the toilet and clean themselves?Reminders, escort, hands-on help
ContinenceAre bladder and bowel controlled?Pads, scheduled toileting, changing at night
Transfers and mobilityCan they get in and out of bed and chairs, and walk safely?Walker, wheelchair, one-person assist, two-person assist (often beyond assisted living)
EatingCan they feed themselves?Cutting food, cueing, a modified diet, help to eat
MedicationsCan they take the right pills at the right time?Reminders, staff administering every dose, injections, eye drops
Memory and behaviourAre they oriented, safe, calm?Reminders and redirection, night checks, behaviour support, secured unit

Alongside these, assessors note the tasks of running a home, called instrumental activities of daily living: cooking, shopping, housework, laundry, money, the phone and transport. In assisted living most of these are covered by the base rate, so they affect the decision to move more than the care charge.

What happens at the assessment

  1. Before the visit: the community asks for the physician's report, diagnoses and medication list, and sometimes recent hospital or therapy notes.
  2. The visit: a nurse or wellness director meets your parent at home, in hospital or at the community. They watch your parent walk and stand, ask about each activity, and talk to the family.
  3. The score: each need is scored by how much help and how often. Some communities use a levels table, others count points or minutes of staff time.
  4. The result: a care level, the monthly charge for it, and a service plan saying what staff will do and when.
  5. The decision: the community confirms whether it can meet your parent's needs under its licence. If it cannot, it should say so plainly and suggest the right level.

Ask for the result in writing, with the service plan, before you sign the residency agreement.

Why the level changes the price

Staff time is the main cost of assisted living. A resident who needs help to shower twice a week and reminders for medications takes far less staff time than a resident who needs help to dress every morning, an escort to every meal, and checks through the night. Care levels are how the community prices that difference.

There are three common models:

  • Levels: level one, two, three and so on, each adding a fixed monthly amount.
  • Points: each task carries points; the total maps to a monthly charge.
  • All-inclusive: one rate covers all care the community provides, so the bill does not jump with each change in needs.

When you compare communities, compare the total at your parent's assessed level, not the base rate. Our cost guide shows how to compare quotes fairly.

Be honest in the assessment

Parents often understate what they need, especially in front of a stranger. Families sometimes do too, hoping for a lower care level. Both backfire.

  • A care level set too low means staff are scheduled for less help than your parent needs. Care suffers in the first weeks, which are already the hardest.
  • The community will reassess quickly once staff see the real picture, and the bill will rise anyway.
  • If the real needs are beyond what the community can meet, you will be facing another move.

Before the visit, write a page describing an ordinary day and an ordinary night: what your parent does alone, what they need prompting for, what they need hands-on help with, and anything that has happened recently such as falls, missed medications or getting lost. Give a copy to the assessor.

When reassessment happens

Care levels are not fixed. Communities reassess:

  • After a hospital stay, a fall or an illness.
  • When staff notice your parent needs more help, or less.
  • At regular intervals set out in the agreement, often every few months or yearly.
  • When the family asks.

Ask how much notice you will get before a new care level changes the bill, whether you can see the reassessment, and whether you can ask for it to be reviewed. Needs can also go down, for example after rehab, and the level should then drop.

When needs go beyond assisted living

Assisted living in Tennessee is licensed to help with daily activities and medications, not to provide round-the-clock skilled nursing. Needs that often go beyond it:

  • Transfers that need two staff or a mechanical lift.
  • Daily skilled nursing such as complex wound care, IV medicines or frequent injections that the resident cannot manage.
  • Being bedbound, except under hospice.
  • Behaviour that puts the resident or others at risk and that the community cannot manage, even in a secured unit.

Each community decides within its licence. If your parent is close to any of these, ask before you sign what would happen, and read the discharge section of the residency agreement. Our guides to levels of care and the residency agreement cover this.

ADLs and long-term care insurance

The same activities matter for insurance. Most long-term care insurance policies start paying when a licensed health professional certifies that the insured person needs help with at least two activities of daily living, or needs supervision because of severe cognitive impairment. The community's assessment can support a claim; ask for a copy. Our paying for care guide covers claims.

How to prepare for the assessment

  • A current medication list, including over-the-counter medicines and supplements.
  • Diagnoses and the name and number of each doctor.
  • Your one-page description of an ordinary day and night.
  • Recent hospital discharge papers or therapy notes, if any.
  • Mobility aids your parent uses: walker, cane, wheelchair.
  • Dietary needs and allergies.
  • Who holds power of attorney for health care and finances.

Questions to ask

  • Do you price care by levels, points or all-inclusive?
  • Which tasks put my parent at this level, and what is the monthly charge?
  • What would move my parent to the next level, and how much would that add?
  • How often do you reassess, and how much notice before a change to the bill?
  • Can I see the written assessment and the service plan?
  • Which needs could you not meet under your licence?

An example of how a level is set

Consider a parent who walks with a walker, needs stand-by help in the shower three times a week, needs every medication handed to them and watched, is continent, dresses with reminders, and is oriented but forgetful. Most communities would score that as a low to middle care level: medication administration and bathing help are the main tasks.

Now add a hip fracture. After rehab, the same parent needs one person to help with every transfer, help dressing every morning, help to the toilet at night and an escort to meals. The care level jumps by several steps, and the monthly bill with it, even though the apartment and the base rate have not changed.

And if dementia progresses so that your parent tries to leave the building, the community will look at its secured unit, which is often priced differently again. This is why families should ask how each step is priced before move-in, not after the first reassessment.

The tasks of running a home

Professionals call them instrumental activities of daily living: using the phone, shopping, preparing food, housekeeping, laundry, transport, handling medications and managing money. They are usually the first things a parent struggles with, often years before help with bathing or dressing is needed. Unpaid bills, an empty fridge, missed appointments and a car with new dents are typical early signs.

In assisted living, most of these are covered by the base rate: meals, housekeeping, linen laundry and scheduled transport. Medication management is usually priced as part of care. Money management is not something communities take on; a family member with financial power of attorney usually does.

If you disagree with the assessment

Ask the nurse to walk you through each item and the evidence for it. Bring your one-page description and any notes from your parent's doctor or therapists. If you still disagree, ask for a reassessment after two to four weeks, when staff have seen your parent day to day. A good community will explain its scoring openly.

Do not forget the night

Assessments often focus on the morning routine, because that is when most help is given. The night matters as much. Ask yourself, and tell the assessor: does your parent get up to use the toilet, and are they steady when they do? Do they wander or become confused after dark? Do they need repositioning, changing or reassurance overnight? Have any of the falls happened at night?

Night-time needs decide whether a community's overnight staffing is enough for your parent, and they often push the care level up. Communities differ a great deal in how many staff are awake overnight, so knowing your parent's night-time needs also tells you which questions to ask about staffing on a tour. Our tour questions include the ones to ask.

A short diary for a week before the assessment, noting each time your parent needed help at night and with what, gives the nurse something concrete to score.

faq.q: What are the activities of daily living?
faq.a: The basic personal tasks of looking after yourself: bathing, dressing, eating, using the toilet, staying continent, and moving from bed to chair. Assisted living communities also assess medication management, memory and behaviour.

faq.q: Who does the assisted living assessment?
faq.a: Usually the community's nurse or wellness director. They review the physician's report and medication list, meet your parent, and talk with the family before setting a care level and service plan.

faq.q: How does the care level affect the price?
faq.a: Each care level, or points total, adds a monthly charge on top of the base rate because it reflects staff time. A higher level means a higher bill, unless the community uses an all-inclusive rate.

faq.q: How often is a resident reassessed?
faq.a: After hospital stays, falls or a change in needs, at intervals set in the residency agreement, and when the family asks. Ask how much notice you get before a new level changes the bill.

faq.q: Should we play down our parent's needs to get a lower price?
faq.a: No. An understated assessment means staff plan for less help than your parent needs, care suffers in the first weeks, and the community will reassess and raise the bill anyway.

faq.q: What needs are usually beyond assisted living?
faq.a: Transfers needing two staff or a lift, daily skilled nursing such as complex wound care or IV medicines, being bedbound outside hospice, and behaviour the community cannot manage safely.

faq.q: Do activities of daily living matter for long-term care insurance?
faq.a: Yes. Most policies start paying when a licensed professional certifies the insured person needs help with at least two activities of daily living, or has severe cognitive impairment.
